comments.author: @pnnyfryrthghts
comments.text:
People aren't aware but after the end of the Spanish-American war (1898), the Philippines was actually a US territory, along with Guam and Puerto Rico, until Japan took hold of it in 1942. And after finally became an independent country with its own Constitution. 

Had they decided to remain a US territory, the odds of Filipinos moving elsewhere for work (OFW) likely wouldn't be as massive as it is today because American companies likely would have expanded there creating even more jobs and increase in manufactured goods. Guam was ideal post-WW2 because it's a US territory that was looking for workers to help reconstruct the island. It was nearby and most of all, had a link to its past during the Spanish Empire (Mexico City, Guam, Manila).

comments.author: @russandrada3776
comments.text: Guam was historically connected to the Spanish Philippines through colonial administration, trade, religion, and migration. But Guam has its own indigenous CHamoru identity and is geographically part of Micronesia. So the video title about Filipinos finding the American Dream in Guam is understandable: Guam has a long historical relationship with the Philippines, and today it offers many Filipinos opportunities to work and live in an American territory.

comments.author: @raiderfel
comments.text:
There is a lot of misinformation, exaggeration, and outright contradictions in this video about Guam and the Filipino community here.
First, we don’t all speak Tagalog—Guam’s Filipino community has deep, multi-generational roots in Ilocos and Iloilo, so Ilocano and Hiligaynon (Ilonggo) are widely spoken here alongside Tagalog and English. Thousands of Ilonggos helped rebuild Guam after WWII through Camp Roxas in Agat/Santa Rita, and their families have been established U.S. citizens and permanent residents for decades—not temporary workers trying to get "anchor babies."
The script also constantly contradicts itself—claiming everyone is barely surviving on $9.25 minimum wage in cramped rooms, while also acknowledging that nurses, business owners, and established middle-class families live here, and ignoring that H-2B workers are legally paid prevailing wages ($14–$21+/hr) with employer-provided housing. Plus, the Jones Act only applies to U.S.-to-U.S. shipping, not direct cargo ships from Asia. Guam has real challenges with cost of living and infrastructure, but reducing our history and community to AI-scripted poverty tropes misses the reality of life here.
